```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaBio)
```

`cudaBio` is a small downstream example of the `rcupp` framework. It computes
principal components by power iteration using the fixed GPU operators reached
through `LinkingTo: rcupp`. It contains no CUDA code of its own, so it runs
unchanged whether `rcupp` was built with a CUDA backend or its CPU shim.

## A first decomposition

```{r pca}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60 * 5), 60, 5)

pca <- cuda_pca(X, ncomp = 2)
pca$values
```

The result is a list with the leading eigenvalues (`values`), the column
`loadings`, the per-observation `scores`, and the number of power iterations
(`iters`):

```{r shapes}
dim(pca$loadings)
dim(pca$scores)
pca$iters
pca$backend
```

The loadings are unit vectors in the original feature space; the scores are
the projected data. As with all `rcupp` consumers, `backend` is reported for
information only and does not affect the result.

## A worked example: population structure

A typical bioinformatics use of PCA is to reveal population structure in a
matrix of genetic markers. Here three cohorts differ along two latent
directions; `cuda_pca()` should recover that structure without being told the
labels.

```{r cohorts}
set.seed(42)
cohorts <- c("Cohort A", "Cohort B", "Cohort C")
group <- rep(cohorts, each = 40)
n <- length(group)
p <- 30

v1 <- rnorm(p)
v2 <- rnorm(p)
shift1 <- c(-3, 0, 3)[match(group, cohorts)]
shift2 <- c(2, -2, 1)[match(group, cohorts)]
X <- outer(shift1, v1) + outer(shift2, v2) +
  matrix(rnorm(n * p, sd = 0.5), n, p)
colnames(X) <- paste0("marker", seq_len(p))

pca <- cuda_pca(X, ncomp = 4)
pca$backend
```

The loadings are unit length and the eigenvalues decrease with each deflation
step, as expected from power iteration:

```{r checks}
round(sqrt(colSums(pca$loadings^2)), 6)
round(pca$values, 1)
```

### Scree plot

`values` are the eigenvalues `||A v||^2` of the deflated matrix. Dividing by
`sum(X^2)` (the trace of `X'X`, i.e. the total sum of squares) gives the
fraction of variation explained by each component.

```{r scree, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
frac <- pca$values / sum(X^2)
barplot(100 * frac, names.arg = paste0("PC", seq_along(frac)),
        ylab = "Variation explained (%)", col = "steelblue",
        main = "Scree plot")
```

### Sample scores

Projecting each sample onto the first two components separates the three
cohorts, which is exactly the structure PCA is used to detect in genotype
data.

```{r scores, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
cols <- c("steelblue", "darkorange", "seagreen")
idx <- match(group, cohorts)
plot(pca$scores[, 1], pca$scores[, 2], col = cols[idx], pch = 19,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "Sample scores")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey")
legend("topright", legend = cohorts, col = cols, pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

### Loadings

The loadings are the per-marker weights of each component. A heat map shows
which markers drive the separation along the leading components.

```{r loadings, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
nr <- nrow(pca$loadings)
nc <- ncol(pca$loadings)
image(seq_len(nr), seq_len(nc), pca$loadings, axes = FALSE,
      xlab = "Marker", ylab = "Component",
      col = hcl.colors(32, "Blue-Red 3"),
      main = "Loadings by component")
axis(1)
axis(2, at = seq_len(nc), labels = paste0("PC", seq_len(nc)), las = 1)
box()
```

These plots use only base R graphics, so the vignette needs no plotting
package beyond `knitr` and `rmarkdown`.

## Why there is no GPU code here

The package only includes `rcupp`'s public C header and calls the operators
at run time. That is the point of the framework: a downstream package needs
no toolkit, no device memory handling, and no CPU fallback logic of its own.
